html:
Impressionism was an art movement of the late 1800s, led by a group of painters in Paris, who tried to catch light and passing moments with quick, visible brushstrokes. Their first group show in 1874 is often seen as the start of modern art.

The core members were Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Camille Pissarro, Alfred Sisley, Edgar Degas and Berthe Morisot. The official Paris Salon, run by the Academy, favoured smooth, finished paintings of history and myth, and kept rejecting their work. So in 1874 they put on their own exhibition.

A critic mocked Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, a hazy view of the port of Le Havre, and called the group "Impressionists". They took up the name.

What was new:

  • Painting outdoors, directly from nature, made easier by paint sold in tubes.
  • Short strokes of pure colour placed side by side, not blended, so the eye mixes them.
  • Everyday modern subjects: cafés, boating parties, railway stations, the new boulevards of Haussmann's Paris.
  • Shadows painted in colour, not brown or black, and the same subject painted at different times of day.

Photography, which could now record a scene exactly, pushed painters to do something else, and Japanese prints, popular in Paris (see Japonisme), showed them new ways to frame a picture.

They held eight group shows up to 1886. At first they sold little; later, American buyers made them famous. Post-Impressionists such as Van Gogh and Cézanne pushed their ideas further, which led on to Picasso and abstract art.
sum: Impressionism was an art movement of the late 1800s, led by a group of painters in Paris, who tried to catch light and passing moments with quick, visible brushstrokes. Their first group show in 1874 is often seen as the start of modern art…
